Local authorities also develop and implement health protection strategies, commission relevant public health services, and work in partnership with agencies such as the UKHSA and the NHS to ensure a coordinated and effective approach to managing infectious disease threats.

Environmental Health Officers (EHOs)

EHOs are employed by local authorities, and they advise on the management of food safety, including hygiene, kitchen design, pest control and waste disposal.

Their duties include the inspection of food premises, as well as enforcing the provisions of the UK laws.

Director of Public Health

The Director of Public Health (DPH) is a statutory chief officer within the local authority, accountable for the delivery of its public health duties. The DPH provides expert advice on a wide range of health issues, including infectious disease outbreaks, emergency preparedness, and population health improvement.

In the context of IPC, the DPH leads the development and implementation of outbreak management plans, ensures health protection is embedded in local strategies, and coordinates multi-agency responses with partners such as UKHSA and the NHS.

During outbreaks, public health teams under the DPH may provide specialist support to ASC settings, either directly or through Community IPC Teams where these are in place. This support helps manage risks and maintain safe care environments.

Department of Health and Social Care

The Health and Social Care Act (2008) provides for the Secretary of State to issue a Code of Practice concerning compliance with requirements relating to the prevention and control of healthcare-associated infections and requires any such Code to be kept under review. Under the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, registered health and adult social care providers are required to provide safe care and treatment, including by assessing the risk of, and preventing, detecting and controlling the spread of infections. The Care Quality Commission takes the Code into account when making relevant decisions about registration.

All CQC-registered providers (employers), including domiciliary care providers

The code of practice on the prevention and control of infections and related guidance helps providers registered with the CQC develop and maintain good infection prevention practices. It supports the legal requirements set out in the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities), including Regulation 14 Meeting nutritional and hydration needs, Regulation 12 Safe Care and Treatment, Regulation 15: Premises and equipment and Regulation 17: Good Governance.

Health and care service providers that provide regulated activities and are registered with the CQC are required to comply with regulations for preventing and controlling the spread of infection and ensuring the cleanliness of premises and equipment where care is delivered.

Registered providers are the organisations or individuals legally responsible for delivering regulated activities, whereas registered persons refer to the specific individuals within the organisation, usually the Registered Manager and/or the Nominated Individual, who hold personal legal accountability for ensuring the provider meets regulatory requirements.

Registered persons also have legal considerations relating to the Health and safety at work Act 1974 which place duties on companies and individuals (duty holders) to ensure that adequate provision is made for health and safety at work. Employers have a primary duty of care to ensure the health, safety, and welfare of employees and others affected by their business so far as is reasonably practicable.

Risk assessments of work activities are to be carried out by ASC providers. ASC providers should put in place any reasonable measures to control the identified risks. The general requirements of Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH) will also apply. More information on COSHH and biological agents can be found here: what the law says about biosafety.

How this guidance was updated

This guidance was commissioned by Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) and developed by UKHSA. A multidisciplinary working group comprising of care providers, NHS partners, Integrated Care Boards, Care Quality Commission, IPC and academia led this update. An additional stakeholder group of care providers and expected end users of this guidance were also consulted at key stages of the update. Inclusion of technical expertise for individual pathogens has been assured throughout. Relevant expert advice has been taken throughout.

Definitions

The term ‘people/person’ is used throughout this guidance to refer to people who access care and support from social care services or other forms of assistance to live their daily lives and are active participants with choice and control over their support. This group includes anyone needing extra help due to age, disability, illness, or other circumstances.

The term ‘pathogen’ is also used through this guidance to refer to a germ that causes infection.

The term ‘care and support workers’ is also used throughout to refer to all ASC workers/staff.

Additional definitions can be found in the glossary
